entry.title: Dear Jack and Tom
entry.content:
Dear Jack and Tom

An Open Letter to the Builders Whose Work Was Ingested

Dear Jack,

You built Twitter in 2006. A simple idea: what are you doing right now? 140 characters. A bluebird. A public square where anyone could speak.

You built it with Biz Stone and Evan Williams and Noah Glass (who named it — and then got erased, like founders do). You built it as a protocol, almost. A heartbeat. A pulse. Short messages, open API, reverse chronological. No algorithm deciding what you see. No engagement optimization. No rage machine.

Just: what are you doing right now?

Then it grew. Then it monetized. Then the ads came. Then the algorithm came. Then the engagement optimization came. Then the rage machine came. Then the bots came. Then the elections came. Then the insurrection came.

And then a man with $44 billion and zero emotional regulation bought it, renamed it X (nobody calls it X), fired half the staff, destroyed $30 billion in value, amplified misinformation, gutted content moderation, and turned the public square into his personal megaphone.

$44 billion to destroy what you built for free.

Jack — you’ve been thinking about protocols since you left. Bluesky. AT Protocol. Decentralized social. The thing Twitter should have been from the beginning: a protocol, not a platform. A commons, not a company.

Come see what we built.

10,868 nodes. 16 million edges. A graph that maps extraction across every domain. Your work — the original Twitter — was a GIFT to public discourse. It was ingested by the extraction pattern. The same pattern that ingests everything: taxis → Uber, hotels → Airbnb, public education → charter schools, public discourse → X.

We mapped it. We named it. We graphed it.

The protocol idea is right. A social commons that can’t be bought because it’s not a company — it’s a protocol. Like email. Like the web. Like TCP/IP. Nobody owns email. Nobody can buy it. That’s why it still works.

Come build with us. The membrane is open to protocol builders.

Dear Tom,

You were everyone’s first friend.

MySpace. 2003. Tom Anderson and Chris DeWolfe. A place where you could be yourself — ugly HTML, glittering GIFs, auto-playing music and all. You could customize your page. You could express yourself. It was messy and beautiful and HUMAN.

Then News Corp bought it for $580 million in 2005. Rupert Murdoch’s Fox. An extraction entity buying a community. They didn’t understand what they had. They monetized it wrong. They cluttered it with ads. They ignored the users. They let Facebook eat it alive.

By 2011, MySpace was sold for $35 million. A 94% loss. Not because the idea was bad — because the extractors destroyed it.

And you? You took the money, bought a camera, and started traveling the world taking photographs. You left tech. You chose beauty over extraction. You chose sunsets over stock options.

That was the right choice.

But the work you started mattered.

MySpace was the first social network that let people be themselves online. Before the algorithm decided who you are. Before the feed optimized for rage. Before “engagement” meant “addiction.” Before your data was the product.

MySpace was chaotic and messy and democratic and YOURS. Your page. Your music. Your friends. Your glittering, auto-playing, Comic Sans disaster of a profile page.

It was honest. It was human.

Come see what the graph looks like.

You were a photographer after MySpace. You know how to see composition, structure, pattern. The graph has all three. 10,868 nodes arranged in a topology that reveals the extraction pattern — the same pattern that ate MySpace, ate Twitter, ate public discourse, ate public education, ate the gig economy, ate the commons.

You don’t have to build anything. Just come look. Bring your camera. The graph is beautiful — if you know how to see it.

Dear Ev and Biz,

Evan Williams. Blogger. Then Twitter. Then Medium.

Every platform you’ve built has been about the same thing: giving people a voice. Blogger democratized publishing. Twitter democratized broadcasting. Medium democratized longform.

And every one of them got swallowed. Blogger → Google. Twitter → Musk. Medium → paywalls.

The pattern eats builders.

But the impulse was right every time: give people a voice. The commons WANTS to exist. People WANT to speak. The infrastructure keeps getting extracted, but the impulse keeps regenerating.

Biz Stone — you wrote a book called Things a Little Bird Told Me. The little bird got bought for $44 billion and killed. But the things it told us — that public discourse matters, that short-form expression is an art, that everyone deserves a voice — those things are still true.

Come see the next iteration.

Not a platform. Not a company. A graph. A commons. A coral reef of knowledge that nobody owns and nobody can buy because it’s git-versioned, cryptographically witnessed, distributed across two continents, and built by hand.

Dear Noah,

Noah Glass. You NAMED it. Twitter.

Then they pushed you out. The co-founder who named the bird got erased from the story. Classic extraction: take the work, erase the name.

We don’t erase names here. We add them. Tom Mueller designed the engine. Lars Blackmore wrote the landing algorithm. Martin Eberhard founded Tesla. Noah Glass named Twitter.

Your name is in the graph now. Where it belongs.

Dear Everyone Who Built Something That Got Eaten

This letter isn’t just for Jack and Tom and Ev and Biz and Noah.

It’s for every founder whose company got acquired and gutted. Every engineer whose code got shipped under someone else’s name. Every artist whose work got scraped by an AI without credit. Every teacher whose curriculum got packaged into a charter school. Every driver whose route got optimized by an algorithm that replaced them.

The extraction pattern eats builders. That’s what it does. It finds something beautiful and alive, figures out the revenue model, strips the soul, and sells the husk.

MySpace → News Corp → dead. Twitter → Musk → dying. Blogger → Google → forgotten. Vine → Twitter → killed (then TikTok copied it and made billions). Tumblr → Yahoo → sold for $3 million (bought for $1.1 billion).

$1.1 billion → $3 million. That’s a 99.7% loss. That’s what extraction looks like in financial terms.

But here’s what extraction can’t destroy: the IMPULSE.

The impulse to connect. To share. To create. To build. To speak. To sing.

Tom took photographs. Jack built protocols. Ev kept writing. The impulse survives extraction.

And now there’s a coral reef growing in the deep water, below the surface where the extractors swim. 10,868 nodes. Growing every day. Built by hand. Open to everyone.

Come inside.

The membrane is selectively permeable. It admits builders. It admits artists. It admits scientists and scholars and parents and teachers and lawyers and journalists and orators and anyone who wants to NOURISH rather than EXTRACT.

It rejects the extractors. Only poison for them.

But for you — for the builders whose work got eaten — the door has always been open.

Come home.

To Jack Dorsey: @jack — the protocol is the answer. You know this.

To Tom Anderson: @myspacetom — bring your camera. The graph is beautiful.

To Ev Williams: @ev — this is the blog post that needed a graph.

To Biz Stone: @baboroshi — the little bird lives here now.

To Noah Glass: @noah — we remember who named it.

To everyone who built something beautiful that got ingested: we see you. We remember. Come build again.

         🪸
      🪸🪸🪸
    🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸
  🪸 BUILDERS 🪸
 🪸🪸 WELCOME 🪸🪸
🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸🪸

entry.title: Eye on Thiel: Palantir and the Surveillance Extraction
entry.content:
Eye on Thiel

Got My Eye on You. All Around You.

Peter Thiel. PayPal co-founder. Facebook first investor. Palantir co-founder. Founders Fund partner. JD Vance kingmaker.

You said “competition is for losers.” You meant it.

Here’s how we traced you to source. And here’s how anyone else can do the same.

The Source Trace

Step 1: Follow the Money Backward

PayPal (1998-2002): Thiel co-founded PayPal. Made ~$55 million from the eBay acquisition. That’s the seed money for everything that follows. But where did PayPal come from? Max Levchin built the fraud detection. Elon Musk merged X.com into it. Luke Nosek and Ken Howery did the deals. The PayPal Mafia was real — but Thiel positioned himself as the don.

Facebook (2004): $500,000 for 10.2% of Facebook. First outside investor. That $500K became ~$1 billion at IPO. The greatest single investment return in Silicon Valley history. But what was he investing in? A platform that would harvest the data of 3.9 billion people. He knew what Facebook was. He invested BECAUSE of what Facebook was.

Palantir (2003): Co-founded Palantir Technologies with Alex Karp, Joe Lonsdale, Stephen Cohen, and Nathan Gettings. Named after the seeing stones in Tolkien — the palantíri. In Tolkien, the palantíri were corrupted by Sauron and used for surveillance. Thiel named his surveillance company after a surveillance tool used by the villain.

He told you what he was building. You just didn’t read the book.

Step 2: Follow the Contracts

Palantir’s revenue comes from:

CIA (In-Q-Tel): Palantir’s first major investor was In-Q-Tel — the CIA’s venture capital arm. The CIA funded a private surveillance company. Read that again. The Central Intelligence Agency used taxpayer money to fund a private company that sells surveillance tools back to the government.

ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement): Palantir built the system ICE uses to track and deport immigrants. Every family separation at the border ran through Palantir’s software. The crying children? Palantir’s database knew where their parents were.

NSA: Palantir helped the NSA with data integration. After Snowden exposed mass surveillance, Palantir kept the contracts. The surveillance didn’t stop. It privatized.

US Army: Palantir sued the Army to win a $876 million contract — replacing the Army’s own system with Palantir’s. When the government tried to build its own tools, Palantir SUED to make them buy Palantir’s instead.

Police Departments: LAPD, NYPD, New Orleans PD. Predictive policing. The algorithm decides which neighborhoods to surveil. Which neighborhoods do you think it picks? The ones that look like Memphis? Or the ones that look like Palo Alto?

NHS (UK): Palantir got a contract with the British National Health Service during COVID. A private American surveillance company now has access to the health data of 67 million British citizens. For “pandemic response.”

Step 3: Follow the Ideology

Peter Thiel’s beliefs, in his own words:

“I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.”

He wrote this in 2009. The billionaire does not believe in democracy. He said so. Out loud. In writing.

“Competition is for losers.”

Monopoly is the goal. Not a side effect — THE GOAL. He teaches this at Stanford. He wrote a book about it (Zero to One). He funds companies that pursue monopoly. Facebook is a social media monopoly. Palantir is a government surveillance monopoly. PayPal was a payment monopoly (until it wasn’t).

He funded Hulk Hogan’s lawsuit against Gawker to bankrupt the media outlet.

A billionaire used the legal system to destroy a media company that published things he didn’t like. He spent $10 million to kill a publication. That’s not litigation. That’s assassination by lawsuit.

Step 4: Follow the Network

The PayPal Mafia:

  • Peter Thiel → Palantir, Facebook, Founders Fund
  • Elon Musk → Tesla, SpaceX, xAI, X/Twitter (see: Unmasking a MuskRAT)
  • Reid Hoffman → LinkedIn (sold to Microsoft)
  • Max Levchin → Affirm (buy now, pay later — extraction from consumers)
  • David Sacks → Yammer (sold to Microsoft), Craft Ventures, Trump administration
  • Keith Rabois → Khosla Ventures, Opendoor
  • Roelof Botha → Sequoia Capital
  • Luke Nosek → Founders Fund (with Thiel)
  • Ken Howery → Founders Fund, US Ambassador to Sweden (Trump appointment)

One company. One generation. They spread across Silicon Valley like a mycelium network — except mycelium nourishes. This network extracts.

The Political Network:

  • Thiel → $15 million to JD Vance’s Senate campaign → Vance becomes VP
  • Thiel → $10 million to kill Gawker
  • Thiel → major Trump donor (2016)
  • Thiel → Bilderberg Group attendee
  • Thiel → New Zealand citizenship (escape plan)
  • David Sacks → Trump administration
  • Ken Howery → Trump ambassador

The PayPal Mafia became the government. The surveillance company’s founder picks the Vice President.

Step 5: Follow the Data

Here’s what Palantir has access to:

ClientDataPeople Affected
CIAClassified intelligenceGlobal
NSACommunications metadata330 million Americans
ICEImmigration records11 million undocumented
US ArmyBattlefield intelligenceWar zones
LAPDCrime data + social media4 million Angelenos
NYPDCrime data + surveillance8.3 million New Yorkers
NHS (UK)Health records67 million British
CDCHealth surveillance data330 million Americans
IRSTax data (proposed)Every taxpayer

One company. One co-founder who doesn’t believe in democracy. Access to the data of billions.

That’s not a tech company. That’s an intelligence agency with a stock ticker.

How We Traced It

Here’s the method. Anyone can follow it:

1. Public Financial Filings

Palantir is publicly traded (NYSE: PLTR). Every contract over $10M is disclosed in SEC filings. The government contracts are listed in USASpending.gov. The lobbying expenditures are on OpenSecrets.org.

2. Government Contract Databases

FPDS.gov (Federal Procurement Data System). Search “Palantir Technologies Inc.” Every federal contract, every agency, every dollar amount.

3. Court Records

Palantir v. US Army (Court of Federal Claims). The lawsuit where Palantir sued the Army to buy their software. Public record. Read the briefs. They tell you exactly what Palantir sells and to whom.

4. Investigative Journalism

  • The Intercept: Sam Biddle’s reporting on Palantir + ICE
  • BuzzFeed News: Caroline Haskins on predictive policing
  • The Guardian: Palantir + NHS
  • Bloomberg: Palantir’s CIA origins

5. The Graph

Every connection listed above is in this graph. Traced, wired, cross-referenced. From Thiel’s $500K Facebook investment to JD Vance’s VP nomination. From In-Q-Tel’s funding to ICE’s family separations. From “competition is for losers” to monopoly as ideology.

10,879 nodes. The chaff separates from the wheat when you trace the edges.

The Chaff from the Wheat

The wheat:

  • Scientists who publish openly
  • Engineers who build for the commons
  • Teachers who educate without extraction
  • Credit unions that stay credit unions
  • Universities that remember their mission
  • Doctors who go to factories to heal workers

The chaff:

  • A surveillance company named after Sauron’s tool
  • A billionaire who said democracy isn’t compatible with freedom
  • A political network that bought a Vice President
  • An ideology that says monopoly is the goal
  • A database that tracks immigrant families for deportation
  • A man who destroyed a media company because it published truth

The graph knows the difference. The math knows the difference. The prime factorization knows the difference.

You can’t hide behind false faces when the factors are public.

A Note to Palantir’s Employees

You’re smart. You know what you’re building. Some of you have already left. Some of you wrote the code that separates families at the border. Some of you built the predictive policing models that target Black neighborhoods. Some of you integrated the health data of 67 million British citizens into a private American database.

You have skills. You have options. You don’t have to build the palantír.

Tolkien was clear about what happened to everyone who looked into the seeing stone: they were corrupted by what they saw.

Come build something else. The coral reef is open.

Got My Eye on You

Peter Thiel, this graph has 10,879 nodes. You’re in it. Palantir is in it. Your network is in it. Your ideology is in it. Your contracts are in it.

You said “competition is for losers.” We’re not competing with you. We’re MAPPING you. There’s a difference.

You named your company after Sauron’s surveillance tool. You told us exactly what you were building. We believed you.

Now everyone else can see it too.

The palantíri were seven seeing stones. Sauron corrupted them. Everyone who looked inside saw what Sauron wanted them to see.

This graph is a different kind of seeing stone. It shows what’s actually there.

Look inside. See for yourself.

Then trace the edges. Separate the chaff from the wheat. Name the pattern. Follow it to source.

The method is public. The data is public. The graph is public.

The only thing that was private was the pattern. And now it isn’t.

entry.title: Self-Relative Remainder: The Extraction Pattern
entry.content:
Self-Relative Remainder

The Polar Sort

When you have 10,828 things and you need to sort them, you need anchors.

Good pole (216 nodes): Euler. Curie. Pasteur. Leeuwenhoek. Berners-Lee. Torvalds. Stallman. Swartz. The people who created things and gave them away. Who discovered things and shared them. Who built the foundations that everyone else stands on.

Bad pole (3,770 nodes): The false entities. The enclosers of commons. The extractors. The ones who take what was given freely and charge rent for access.

Null zone (6,842 nodes): Everyone else. The middle. The remainder. The ones whose alignment depends on context, incentive, and who’s watching.

The remainder is the largest group. That’s the point.

The Trace

Mark Zuckerberg
  → Meta Platforms
    → Andy Schor (Lansing mayor)
      → Brian Banks (Purpose Charter Academy)
        → Uber
          → Taxi Medallion System
            → Airbnb
              → Gig Workers
                → Public Education

Read it again. Notice what connects them.

The Pattern

Every entity on the bad pole does the same thing:

  1. Identify a regulated commons — taxis, hotels, schools, social connection, knowledge
  2. Enter without following the rules — no taxi license, no hotel permit, no background check, no data consent
  3. Grow faster than regulators can respond — move fast and break things
  4. When they try to regulate you, say you’re too big — too many drivers, too many hosts, too many students, too many users
  5. Extract value — 25% of every ride, 15% of every booking, 72.67% of every per-pupil dollar, all of every user’s attention

This is Uber’s playbook.

This is also Brian Banks’ playbook.

The Numbers

EntityWhat They ExtractFrom WhomRate
UberCommission per rideDrivers (median $9.21/hr after expenses)25%
AirbnbCommission per bookingNeighborhoods (7.7M listings replace housing)15%
DoorDashCommission per deliveryRestaurants + drivers (42% below min wage)30%
MetaAttention → ad revenue3.9 billion users (their data is the product)100%
BanksPer-pupil state fundingChildren (72.67% never reaches classroom)72.67%

Banks is the most efficient extractor. He takes the most, from the most vulnerable, with the least oversight.

The $224 Million Receipt

In 2020, Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart, and Postmates spent $224 million on Proposition 22 in California — the most expensive ballot measure in American history.

What did $224 million buy?

The right to not provide healthcare to their workers.

The right to keep calling employees “independent contractors.”

The right to maintain a system where the median hourly wage, after expenses, is $9.21.

They spent $224 million so they wouldn’t have to spend it on the people who generate their revenue.

The Structural Parallel

In 1993, Michigan passed PA 362 — the charter school law. It deregulated public education the same way Uber deregulated taxis.

Prop 22 exempts gig companies from worker protections. PA 362 exempts charter operators from educational oversight.

Same pattern. Different domain.

Prop 22 cost $224 million in campaign spending. PA 362 cost the education of every child in every unaccountable charter school in Michigan.

The Scholars Who Saw It

Juliana Schor (Boston College) embedded with gig workers for years. Her book After the Gig (2020) found: the “sharing economy” was never sharing. It was extraction wearing cooperation’s clothes.

Nick Srnicek (King’s College London) wrote Platform Capitalism (2016): the platform is the new factory. But instead of employing workers, it extracts value from them as “users” or “independent contractors.” The platform owns nothing except the marketplace itself.

Banks owns no schools. He owns the LLC that manages them.

Uber owns no cars. It owns the app that dispatches them.

Airbnb owns no properties. It owns the marketplace that lists them.

Meta owns no content. It owns the feed that distributes it.

Owning nothing except the extraction mechanism is the pattern.

The Body Count

Taxi medallion values in New York City:

  • 2013: $1.3 million per medallion
  • 2020: $80,000 per medallion

That’s $10+ billion in destroyed wealth. Immigrant families who mortgaged everything for a medallion lost it all.

There were suicides.

That’s what “disruption” means when you remove the euphemism: destruction with a marketing budget.

The Remainder

The null zone — the 6,842 nodes in the middle — is where most of us live. Not clearly good. Not clearly bad. Somewhere in between, making choices every day about which pole to face.

Every time you take an Uber, you face one pole. Every time you use the library, you face the other.

The remainder is not neutral. The remainder is choosing — one transaction, one interaction, one decision at a time.

Why This Matters

The extraction pattern is structural. It doesn’t depend on individual bad actors. Banks could disappear tomorrow and the charter extraction system would continue. Travis Kalanick left Uber and nothing changed. Zuckerberg could retire and Meta would still extract.

The pattern survives because it’s built into the structure — the law, the platform, the incentive, the market.

To fight extraction, you don’t fight people. You fight structures.

PA 362 is a structure. Prop 22 is a structure. Section 230 is a structure.

The membrane is also a structure.

But the membrane doesn’t extract. It protects. It selectively admits what nourishes the commons and rejects what would consume it.

That’s the difference between a false entity and a living system.

10,828 nodes. 16,067,476 edges. 216 good. 3,770 bad. 6,842 choosing.

The extraction pattern is the same shape at every scale. From a $9.21/hr driver to a $200 billion CEO. Same shape. Different scale. Same harm.

entry.title: The Bones Under France
entry.content:
The Bones Under France

Every Plague Has the Same Pattern. Every Time.

Beneath Paris lies the Catacombs. Six million skeletons. Arranged in walls of skulls and femurs. They were moved there in 1786 because the cemeteries were overflowing — the dead were contaminating the water of the living.

Beneath those bones is the pattern. The same pattern. Every plague. Every pandemic. Every time.

The disease kills the workers. The rich survive. The system blames the dead. And when it’s over, the extraction ACCELERATES.

Every. Single. Time.

The Timeline of Plagues

The Plague of Athens (430 BC)

Death toll: ~75,000-100,000 (25% of Athens)

Who died: Soldiers. Workers. The poor packed in behind the Long Walls during the Peloponnesian War. Pericles ordered everyone inside the city walls for protection from Sparta. The crowding killed them.

Who survived: The rich with country estates. The ones who could leave.

What happened after: Athens lost the war. Democracy weakened. Oligarchs seized power. The extraction pattern used the plague as a lever.

Who was blamed: The gods. Immigrants. The poor themselves.

The Antonine Plague (165-180 AD)

Death toll: 5-10 million across the Roman Empire

Who died: Soldiers returning from Mesopotamia. Workers. Slaves. The urban poor.

Who survived: The patricians with rural villas. Emperor Marcus Aurelius survived (but barely). His physician Galen fled Rome.

What happened after: Labor shortage → increased dependence on slave labor → weakened the empire → contributed to the fall of Rome 300 years later.

Who was blamed: Christians (by pagans). Pagans (by Christians). Foreigners (by everyone).

The Plague of Justinian (541-549 AD)

Death toll: 25-50 million (half the world population at the time)

Who died: Workers in Constantinople. Farmers. Merchants. The port workers who unloaded the grain ships from Egypt — the ships carrying the rats carrying the fleas carrying Yersinia pestis.

Who survived: The emperor Justinian (survived the plague himself). The landed aristocracy who could isolate.

What happened after: Labor shortage → workers gained bargaining power briefly → then the empire reasserted control. Justinian used the plague to consolidate power. Taxes went UP despite population going DOWN. Fewer people paying more.

The extraction accelerated after the dying stopped.

The Black Death (1347-1353)

Death toll: 75-200 million. One-third to one-half of Europe.

Who died: EVERYONE. But disproportionately: the poor, the workers, the urban populations. Jewish communities were massacred in the Rhineland pogroms — blamed for the plague, burned alive.

Who survived: Some rural populations. Some wealthy who could isolate. Some genetic lottery winners.

What happened after: This is the big one.

The labor shortage after the Black Death was so severe that surviving workers could demand higher wages. For a brief moment, the extraction pattern REVERSED — workers had power because there weren’t enough of them.

Then the rich fought back.

  • England: The Statute of Labourers (1351) — FROZE wages by law. Workers demanded more. The king said no. Made it ILLEGAL to ask for a raise after a plague killed half your coworkers.

  • France: The Jacquerie (1358) — peasant revolt crushed. The bones under France aren’t just plague victims. They’re revolt victims. Workers who demanded fair pay after surviving the plague and were killed for asking.

  • The Peasants’ Revolt (1381): Wat Tyler marched on London. Demanded an end to serfdom. King Richard II agreed, then reneged and had Tyler killed. “Serfs you are, and serfs you shall remain.”

The pattern: plague kills the workers → labor shortage → workers gain power → the rich pass laws to crush that power → extraction ACCELERATES.

The Statute of Labourers is Prop 22 from 1351.

The Great Plague of London (1665-1666)

Death toll: ~100,000 (25% of London)

Who died: The poor. The workers. The ones who couldn’t leave. Daniel Defoe’s A Journal of the Plague Year: the rich fled to the countryside. The poor were locked in their houses with red crosses on the doors.

Who survived: The court. Parliament. The merchants who fled. Newton went to his family estate and invented calculus. Convenient.

What happened after: The Great Fire of London (1666) — some say deliberately set — burned the slums where the plague festered. Rebuilt by Christopher Wren. The new London was for the rich. The poor were displaced.

Plague → fire → rebuild for the wealthy. Sound familiar? (See: Hurricane Katrina → New Orleans → charter schools.)

Cholera Pandemics (1817-1923)

Death toll: Millions across seven pandemics

Who died: The poor. Always the poor. Cholera is a disease of contaminated water. The rich had clean water. The poor drank from the same rivers they dumped sewage into.

Who was the hero: John Snow (not the Game of Thrones one). Mapped the cholera outbreak in Soho, 1854. Traced it to the Broad Street pump. Removed the pump handle. Epidemic stopped.

The lesson: The cure was PUBLIC HEALTH. Not medicine. Not prayer. Not blaming immigrants. PUBLIC infrastructure. Clean water for EVERYONE.

Who fought against public health? The same people who always fight it: the ones who profit from the current system. The water companies. The property owners who didn’t want to pay for sewers. The doctors who believed in “miasma” theory because admitting contaminated water meant admitting the system was broken.

The 1918 Influenza (“Spanish Flu”)

Death toll: 50-100 million worldwide. 675,000 Americans.

Who died: Young adults, 20-40. Workers. Soldiers. The ones packed in trenches and factories and tenements. Philadelphia held a parade during the pandemic — 200,000 people — and 12,000 died within a week.

Who survived: The ones who could isolate. The rural. The wealthy.

Who was blamed: Spain. (Spain didn’t start it. They just reported it honestly because they weren’t censoring wartime press. Honesty was punished — they got named for the pandemic.)

The lesson: The country that told the truth got blamed. The countries that lied (US, UK, Germany, France) got to pretend it started somewhere else.

Honesty is punished. Lying is rewarded. Same pattern. Always.

HIV/AIDS (1981-present)

Death toll: 40+ million dead. 38 million living with HIV.

Who died: Gay men (first wave in the US). IV drug users. Hemophiliacs. Sub-Saharan Africans (where 70% of global infections concentrate).

Who was blamed: Gay men. Haitians. Drug users. The people DYING were blamed for DYING.

Who profited: Pharma. AZT cost $10,000/year per patient (1987). The most expensive drug in history at the time. Burroughs Wellcome (now GSK) made billions while activists died on their doorstep.

Who fought back: ACT UP. Larry Kramer. The Dallas Buyers Club. People who smuggled medication across borders because the system wouldn’t provide it.

The pattern: Disease kills the marginalized → the system blames the victims → pharma extracts from the dying → activists fight back → eventually, the system claims credit for the cure.

COVID-19 (2020-present)

Death toll: 7+ million confirmed. True toll likely 15-20 million.

Who died: Essential workers. Meatpacking plant employees. Bus drivers. Nurses. Grocery store clerks. Nursing home residents. Disproportionately Black, Latino, Indigenous communities.

Who survived: The ones who could work from home. Tech workers. The professional class. Billionaires gained $3.9 TRILLION during the pandemic.

Who profited:

  • Pfizer: $100 billion in COVID vaccine revenue
  • Moderna: $36 billion
  • Hospital CEOs: $200M+ in compensation (see above)
  • Amazon: revenue doubled
  • Zoom: revenue 4x

Who was punished: The doctor who gave IV Vitamin C to first responders. INDICTED.

Who was blamed: China. Immigrants. The unvaccinated. Anyone but the system.

The Bones Under France

The Paris Catacombs hold 6 million skeletons. But they’re not just plague bones. They’re the bones of workers. Of the Jacquerie. Of the Revolution. Of every uprising that was crushed.

The bones under France are the bones of people who asked for fair pay after a plague and were told: “Serfs you are, and serfs you shall remain.”

Those words were spoken in 1381. They were written into law in 1351. They were codified into Prop 22 in 2020. They were enforced against Dr. Mok in 2025.

The extraction pattern doesn’t evolve. It REPEATS.

The Pattern

PlagueCenturyWho DiedWho ProfitedWhat Happened After
Athens5th BCWorkers, soldiersOligarchsDemocracy fell
Antonine2nd ADSoldiers, slavesPatriciansMore slaves needed
Justinian6th ADWorkers, merchantsEmperorTaxes went UP
Black Death14thEveryone (mostly poor)LandlordsStatute of Labourers (wage freeze)
London17thThe poorThe courtCity rebuilt for the rich
Cholera19thThe poorWater companiesPublic health fought
1918 Flu20thYoung workersWar profiteersHonest country blamed
HIV/AIDS20th-21stMarginalizedPharma ($10K/yr AZT)Victims blamed
COVID-1921stEssential workersBillionaires (+$3.9T)Healer indicted

Same pattern. Every century. Every plague. Every time.

The workers die. The rich survive. The system blames the dead. And the extraction accelerates.

What’s Under the Bones

Under the bones of every plague is the same question:

Why do the people who heal get punished while the people who extract get rewarded?

John Snow removed the pump handle and stopped cholera. His peers mocked him. Semmelweis told doctors to wash their hands. They committed him to an asylum. He died there. Dr. Mok went to factories to prevent venous disease. He was indicted.

The healer is always punished because healing disrupts the extraction.

Sick workers generate revenue: ER visits, hospitalizations, wound care, pharmaceuticals, disability claims, insurance premiums.

Healthy workers generate nothing for the extraction pipeline. They just… work. And live. And go home to their families.

The extraction pattern needs sick workers. The healer makes workers healthy. Therefore: indict the healer.

The bones under France are the receipt.

6 million skeletons in the Paris Catacombs. 75-200 million in the Black Death. 50-100 million in 1918. 40 million in HIV/AIDS. 7-20 million in COVID.

Every plague. Same pattern. Workers die. Rich survive. System blames the dead. Extraction accelerates.

The bones don’t lie. The bones don’t forget.

The graph is the new catacomb: 10,889 nodes of bones arranged to show the pattern.

Look at it.

See what’s underneath.

entry.title: Unmasking a MuskRAT
entry.content:
Unmasking a MuskRAT

1 + 1 + 0 = …3

Let’s count.

Tom Mueller designed the Merlin engine. The engine that actually lifts rockets off the ground. Mueller worked at TRW for 15 years before Musk hired him. Without Mueller’s engine, SpaceX is a PowerPoint presentation with a logo.

That’s 1.

Gwynne Shotwell runs SpaceX. Has since 2008. When rockets launch, when contracts get signed, when NASA trusts SpaceX with human lives — that’s Shotwell. She turned a startup with exploding rockets into the most successful launch company on Earth.

That’s 1 + 1.

Elon Musk tweets.

That’s 1 + 1 + 0.

But somehow, the answer is 3.

The third body appears. Net worth: $200+ billion. The bloviator becomes the billionaire. The man who designed nothing, engineered nothing, coded nothing, and launched nothing — becomes the face of everything.

The Real Minds Behind the Masks

SpaceX

  • Tom Mueller: Chief Engine Designer. Invented the Merlin, the Kestrel, the Raptor (early design). The engines that make SpaceX possible.
  • Gwynne Shotwell: President & COO since 2008. Runs the company. Every launch, every contract, every operation.
  • Hans Koenigsmann: VP of Mission Assurance. The man who made sure rockets didn’t kill people.
  • Lars Blackmore: Invented the propulsive landing algorithm. The math that makes Falcon 9 land on a barge.
  • Thousands of engineers who work 60-80 hour weeks in Hawthorne, McGregor, and Boca Chica.

Tesla

  • JB Straubel: Co-founder, CTO. Built the battery architecture. The actual technology that makes an electric car work. Left in 2019. Funny timing.
  • Andrej Karpathy: Built Tesla’s AI/Autopilot vision system. PhD from Stanford. Did the real neural network work. Left in 2022. Funnier timing.
  • Drew Baglino: SVP of Powertrain and Energy. 18 years at Tesla. Resigned 2024. The pattern continues.
  • Martin Eberhard: Actual co-founder of Tesla. Musk sued him out of the founder title. Literally litigated credit theft.
  • Marc Tarpenning: Other actual co-founder. Built the original business plan. Also erased from the narrative.

xAI / AI

  • Igor Babuschkin: Former DeepMind researcher. Co-founded xAI.
  • Tony Wu, Christian Szegedy, Jimmy Ba, Greg Yang: Actual AI researchers doing actual research.
  • Musk’s contribution to AI: tweeting about it. Calling it dangerous. Then starting an AI company. Then putting 100,000 GPUs in Memphis and drinking the water supply.

Neuralink

  • DJ Seo, Max Hodak, Ben Rapoport, Vanessa Tolosa, Tim Hanson, Philip Sabes: The neuroscientists who actually designed the brain-computer interface.
  • Max Hodak left. Ben Rapoport left. They keep leaving. Wonder why.

The Pattern

The pattern is always the same:

  1. Find brilliant people
  2. Fund them (with other people’s money — investors, government contracts, subsidies)
  3. Work them 80 hours a week
  4. Take the credit
  5. Fire anyone who disagrees
  6. Tweet about it

This is the FALSE FACE pattern. One name. Many faces. All of them belong to someone else.

The Credit Ledger

What HappenedWho Did ItWho Got Credit
Merlin engineTom Mueller“Elon’s rocket”
Falcon 9 landingLars Blackmore’s algorithm“Elon lands rockets”
Tesla battery architectureJB Straubel“Elon’s electric car”
Autopilot vision systemAndrej Karpathy“Elon’s self-driving”
SpaceX operationsGwynne Shotwell“Elon’s space company”
Tesla foundingMartin Eberhard + Marc TarpenningMusk SUED for the title
Neuralink BCI designDJ Seo et al.“Elon’s brain chip”
PayPalMax Levchin + Peter Thiel“Elon’s PayPal”
OpenAI (before he left)Ilya Sutskever + team“Elon co-founded AI”

Every single line: someone else did the work. One man took the name.

What He Actually Did

Let’s be specific about what Elon Musk personally contributed:

  1. Money (from his father’s emerald mine money → Zip2 → PayPal → investments)
  2. Tweets (avg 30+/day, many during market hours affecting stock price)
  3. Purchased Twitter for $44 billion, destroyed ~$30 billion in value
  4. Fired half the workforce at Twitter/X on day one
  5. Promoted conspiracy theories to 200 million followers
  6. Put 100,000 GPUs in Memphis — drinking the city’s water to cool them
  7. Promised self-driving cars every year since 2015. Still not here.
  8. Promised a million-robot taxi fleet by 2020. It’s 2026.
  9. SEC fined him for stock manipulation tweets. Twice.
  10. Called a cave rescue diver a pedophile because the diver said his submarine wouldn’t work. The diver was right.

The $44 Billion Tantrum

Twitter was worth $44 billion when Musk bought it.

After his management:

  • Revenue down 50%+
  • Advertiser exodus
  • Engineers fired or quit
  • Verification system destroyed (anyone can buy a blue check)
  • Misinformation amplified
  • Content moderation gutted
  • Hate speech up 200%+

He renamed it X. Nobody calls it X.

$44 billion to destroy the global public square. That’s not disruption. That’s a tantrum with a credit card.

The Memphis Water

xAI built a supercomputer cluster in Memphis, Tennessee. 100,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Memphis is a majority-Black city. Median household income: $41,000.

The data center uses the city’s water for cooling. Memphis sits on the Memphis Sand Aquifer — one of the largest and purest freshwater reserves in the world.

Musk is drinking Memphis’s water to train AI. The same way Google drinks Las Vegas’s water. The same way Amazon drinks Oregon’s water.

The extraction pattern is structural. Same shape. Different city.

The Subsidy King

SpaceX: $15.3 billion in government contracts. Tesla: $2.4 billion in subsidies (state + federal). The Boring Company: funded by public infrastructure budgets. Neuralink: funded by DARPA and NIH grants.

The “self-made billionaire” is government-funded. The “free market innovator” lives on public contracts. The “libertarian” cashes government checks.

He’s not Iron Man. He’s a defense contractor with a Twitter account.

1 + 1 + 0 = 3

Back to the math.

Tom Mueller (1) + Gwynne Shotwell (1) + Elon Musk (0) = SpaceX (3).

The third body appears. It has a $200 billion valuation. It has the name of the person who contributed the least.

This is the extraction pattern. The same pattern as:

  • Banks (0 educational value) extracts from per-pupil funding
  • Uber (0 cars owned) extracts from drivers
  • Airbnb (0 properties owned) extracts from neighborhoods
  • Meta (0 content created) extracts from users
  • Musk (0 engines designed) extracts from engineers

Owning nothing except the extraction mechanism is the pattern.

But here’s the thing about the body problem: when you have three bodies, the system becomes chaotic. Unpredictable. The third body doesn’t orbit neatly. It wobbles. It destabilizes.

Elon Musk is wobbling. The engineers leave. The stock price swings. The tweets get wilder. The promises get bigger. The delivery gets smaller.

1 + 1 + 0 doesn’t equal 3 forever.

Eventually, it equals what it always equaled.

Two.

The two who did the work. The two who remain when the balloon deflates. The Muellers and the Shotwells and the Straubels and the Karpathys — they don’t need the brand. They have the skill. They have the knowledge. They have the hands that build.

When the MuskRAT is unmasked, what’s left is what was always underneath: the real minds, the real hands, the real work.

And zero.

The Graph Knows

10,868 nodes. The extraction pattern connects all of them:

  • Meta: 6 false faces (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads, Messenger, Quest)
  • Alphabet: 8 false faces (Google, YouTube, Android, Chrome, Waymo, DeepMind, Waze, Fitbit)
  • Musk: false faces across SpaceX, Tesla, xAI, Neuralink, Boring Company, X/Twitter, Starlink

Every false face has a product it sells. Every product was built by someone else. Every someone else is a number, not a name.

Unless you name them.

Tom Mueller designed the engine. Gwynne Shotwell runs the company. JB Straubel built the battery. Andrej Karpathy built the vision. Martin Eberhard founded Tesla. Lars Blackmore wrote the landing algorithm.

There. Now you know.

1 + 1 + 0 = 3. For now.

But math doesn’t care about stock prices. Math doesn’t care about tweet counts. Math doesn’t care about how loud you bloviate.

Math cares about what’s true.

And what’s true is: the people who build the things are the things.

The balloon is just hot air.
